reviewer: Veteran multi-asset CIO (₹2,000+ Cr family-office/PMS experience)
overall_assessment: This is an unusually rigorous set of documents for a first-pass operating design — the regulatory perimeter is well sourced and appropriately hedged, the Brinson-Fachler/TWRR/XIRR math in the Performance domain is internally exact to the decimal, and the NDPMS consent-latency framing is threaded consistently through Regulatory, Rebalancing, Risk and Operations. But the seven documents were built in parallel and not cross-audited against each other or the two data packs. The most serious problem is a root-caused 100x unit-scaling bug in the Selection domain's TCO model (sel/tco.py) that inflates tax-drag for gold/silver/arbitrage/REIT by 10-25x and drives its headline strategic conclusion. Close behind: Allocation and Risk produce two different GFC/COVID loss estimates for the same portfolios; Risk's own credit-floor limit is breached by Allocation's own Moderate model (AA credit at 16.7% of the FI sleeve vs a 10% ceiling); Allocation's five-sleeve summary table sums to 110% not 100% in both models; and Performance cites the wrong regulation number for client reporting versus three other domains. None of these are fatal to the design's structure, but all would embarrass the team under a sophisticated family office's own spreadsheet audit. There is also a live, unresolved disagreement about what the actual 'Policy Composite' benchmark is between Allocation and Performance — this is the yardstick alpha and fees are judged against and must be a Day-1 decision, not an implicit assumption. A handful of 'hard fact' claims (a custodian AUM exemption threshold, a 2026 MF brokerage-cap reform) are asserted without corroboration in the otherwise thorough verified fact pack and should be treated as unverified until pulled from a primary source before the blueprint is finalized.

findings.target: design_selection.md §9 TCO table; sel/tco.py Gold ETF (8.0*0.10*LTCG*1e4→1,196bps), Silver ETF (8.5*0.20*LTCG*1e4→2,542bps), Arbitrage fund (6.4*0.20*LTCG*1e4→1,914bps), REIT/InvIT LTCG leg (9.5*0.10*LTCG*1e4→1,420 of 1,624bps)
findings.summary: The TCO model's tax-drag formula has a 100x unit-scaling bug for gold, silver, arbitrage and REITs, inflating the domain's headline tax-drag conclusion severalfold.
findings.short_summary: TCO tax-drag has a 100x code bug (gold/silver/arbitrage/REIT)
findings.failure_scenario: Elsewhere in the same script (Nifty, factor, active-MF, direct-equity rows) the tax formula correctly uses decimal-fraction inputs (e.g. 0.05*0.30*LTCG*1e4). For gold/silver/arbitrage/REIT the raw percentage number for expected return (8.0 meaning '8%') is plugged into the same ×1e4 formula, producing a result 100x too large. Recomputed correctly: gold ≈12bps not 1,196; silver ≈25bps not 2,542; arbitrage ≈19bps not 1,914; REIT's LTCG leg ≈14bps (row total ≈218bps) not 1,420 (1,624 total). This drives the reported 317bps portfolio tax drag, 4-7x higher than every other domain's independent estimate (allocation: 60-80bps; performance: 45bps realised; rebalancing's Monte Carlo: 10-50bps at realistic turnover).
findings.suggested_fix: Fix the four affected lines in sel/tco.py (use decimal fractions consistently), rerun, and re-derive the '§9 tax drag dominates' narrative only after the corrected run.

findings.target: design_allocation.md §3.3 (GFC: Mod -29.5%/Agg -39.8%; COVID: Mod -19.7%/Agg -26.8%) vs design_risk.md §3 (GFC: Mod -32.0%/Agg -43.0%; COVID: Mod -22.8%/Agg -28.8%)
findings.summary: GFC- and COVID-type stress-shock estimates for the same Moderate/Aggressive portfolios disagree materially between the two documents that claim to share the same model.
findings.short_summary: Allocation vs Risk give different GFC/COVID loss numbers
findings.failure_scenario: design_risk.md states it reuses 'the same vol/beta/correlation assumptions as the allocation design', yet the two documents' stress outputs for identically-labelled scenarios differ by 2.5-3.5 percentage points on every comparison. A client shown the risk dashboard and the allocation deck in the same meeting sees two different answers to 'how bad could 2008 be for me'. Separately, data_market.md's own 80/20 house-benchmark GFC sizing (-47%) also disagrees with design_allocation's own 80/20 figure (-42.6%).
findings.suggested_fix: Designate one shock-scaling methodology (recommend risk_calc.py's full re-pricing) as canonical and republish design_allocation.md §3.3 to match before either table reaches a client.

findings.target: design_risk.md §1 Limit #7 (AAA/AA+ only, min 90% of FI sleeve) vs design_allocation.md §3.1 Moderate model (AA corporate credit 4% of a 24%-of-AUM FI sleeve)
findings.summary: The Moderate model portfolio breaches the Risk domain's own credit-floor limit on day one.
findings.short_summary: Moderate model breaches its own AA-credit floor limit
findings.failure_scenario: The 4%-of-AUM AA corporate credit line is 4/24 = 16.7% of the 24%-of-AUM FI sleeve, but the house limit requires at least 90% AAA/AA+ (i.e. at most 10% plain-AA). The proposed Moderate model breaches this by ~6.7pp of the FI sleeve before any market move.
findings.suggested_fix: Trim the Moderate AA-credit line to ≤2.4% of AUM (10% of the FI sleeve) or loosen Limit #7 — the two documents must agree before the IPS is signed.

findings.target: design_allocation.md §2.1 five-sleeve table: Moderate (32/33/9/34/2=110%), Aggressive (37/44/12/15/2=110%)
findings.summary: The five-sleeve architecture table sums to 110%, not 100%, in both the Moderate and Aggressive models.
findings.short_summary: Sleeve table sums to 110% not 100% (both models)
findings.failure_scenario: Re-summing the underlying §3.1/§3.2 line items (which do total 100%) shows Satellite alpha should read 23% (Moderate) and 34% (Aggressive), not the 33%/44% printed — a consistent 10pp overstatement in both models' summary table, the kind of basic addition error a client's own analyst checks first.
findings.suggested_fix: Correct the Satellite alpha row to 23% (Moderate) / 34% (Aggressive) so the sleeve table foots to 100%.

findings.target: design_performance.md §0.3/§5.1 'Client reporting floor = PMS Regulations 2020, Regulation 22' vs design_regulatory.md §1.5, design_risk.md and design_operations.md's uniform use of 'Regulation 31'
findings.summary: The client periodic-reporting regulation is cited as Regulation 22 in one domain and Regulation 31 in three others.
findings.short_summary: Reg 22 vs Reg 31 cited inconsistently for client reporting
findings.failure_scenario: A compliance filing or client MITC document that cites the wrong regulation number for its own reporting obligation is a real regulatory-documentation risk; three of the seven domains cannot both be wrong for the same reason, and none independently verified the primary text this session.
findings.suggested_fix: Pull the actual PMS Regulations 2020 text (or one authoritative secondary source) and standardise the regulation number across all seven documents before merge.

findings.target: design_rebalancing.md §5.3 Worked Example B, on-screen route (total '≈₹59 lakh (≈15bps)') and AP route (total '≈₹20 lakh (≈5bps)')
findings.summary: Worked Example B's cost table does not check out arithmetically — a client's own quant would catch this in minutes.
findings.short_summary: Worked Example B bps math is off by ~10x
findings.failure_scenario: ₹59.4 lakh on a ₹40 Cr trade is ≈148bps, not ≈15bps (10x discrepancy); ₹20.4 lakh on the same trade is ≈51bps, not ≈5bps (same pattern). Even the row's own printed component bps (0.1+10+19=29.1) don't sum to its own stated total of 15bps.
findings.suggested_fix: Rebuild Worked Example B from the §5.1 cost-stack table's per-bps assumptions and add a self-check (Σcomponent bps = total; ₹/trade size×10,000 = bps) to future worked examples.

findings.target: design_risk.md §6 'USDINR (spot ~₹88 [design_allocation.md])' vs data_market.md T6 'USDINR ~95.79... verified, 11-Sep-2026'; design_regulatory.md §6 LRS calc at ₹88/USD
findings.summary: The Risk domain's live early-warning dashboard is anchored to a stale/wrong USDINR level (~₹88) against a verified current spot of ₹95.79, an error shared with two other domains.
findings.short_summary: Risk dashboard anchors USDINR at ₹88 vs verified ₹95.79
findings.failure_scenario: The verified data pack in the same project records USDINR at a record-low 95.79 as of 11-Sep-2026 — the date the risk dashboard claims to be current as of. Using ₹88 understates family LRS/GIFT-City headroom by ~8-9% (closer to ₹12 Cr/yr for 5 adults, not ₹11 Cr/yr) and gives the FX early-warning board a wrong reference point from day one.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace every ₹88/USD reference across design_allocation.md, design_regulatory.md and design_risk.md with the verified 95.79 (or a live feed at go-live) and re-run dependent ₹ figures.

findings.target: design_performance.md §2.2 Table 3 (55/7/22/4/4/5/3) vs design_allocation.md §3.3 composite (55/5/25/5/10)
findings.summary: Two different, independently authored 'Policy Composite' benchmarks exist for the same mandate, and neither document acknowledges the other's version.
findings.short_summary: Two conflicting 'Policy Composite' benchmarks exist
findings.failure_scenario: Both are labelled the authoritative T2/mandate benchmark that alpha, fees and the IC scorecard are judged against, yet international (7% vs 5%), fixed income (22% vs 25%), and REIT/AIF treatment (separately benchmarked vs folded into an arbitrage proxy) all differ. This is the yardstick 'owning the returns' depends on.
findings.suggested_fix: Pick one document as source of truth for sleeve weights (recommend Allocation/SAA layer) and regenerate Performance's Table 3 from it exactly, with an explicit sign-off step before the IPS is signed.

findings.target: design_selection.md §9 strategic conclusion ('tax drag dominates... biggest lever is instrument-tax-form selection, not manager alpha'); sel/tco.py tax-drag inputs for short-duration, TMF, G-sec, AA-credit, Cat II, Cat III (E[R]%×tax-rate×100, i.e. full annual realization)
findings.summary: The domain's central strategic conclusion rests on an unrealistic full-annual-realization tax assumption for buy-and-hold sleeves, independent of the code bug in the gold/silver/arbitrage/REIT rows.
findings.short_summary: TCO assumes 100% annual gain realization for hold-to-maturity sleeves
findings.failure_scenario: This modelling choice is dimensionally self-consistent (unlike the 100x bug) but contradicts the 'hold-to-maturity, low-turnover' philosophy in design_allocation and the 4-15%/yr realistic turnover in design_rebalancing's own Monte Carlo. Debt-fund/TMF/AIF gains in a growth structure are not taxed annually — tax crystallizes on redemption, which for a locked AIF or hold-to-maturity TMF could be years away.
findings.suggested_fix: Separate 'cash tax paid this year' (interest/coupon/distributed income, correctly annual) from 'deferred tax on unrealized gains' (crystallizes on redemption) exactly as design_performance's own R3/R4 framework does, and re-run §9.

findings.target: design_operations.md §1.1 'Six voting members... Head of Trading/Ops (non-voting, present for feasibility)...'
findings.summary: The Investment Committee is described as having six voting members, but only five of the six named seats actually vote.
findings.short_summary: IC 'six voting members' claim names only five voters
findings.failure_scenario: Head of Trading/Ops is explicitly marked non-voting, leaving five voting members, not six; a quorum of 4-of-5 (80%) is a materially different governance bar than 4-of-6 (67%).
findings.suggested_fix: Either make Trading/Ops voting or correct the text to 'five voting members, quorum 4' and re-check that quorum bar makes sense at five.

findings.target: design_allocation.md §4 and design_selection.md §1.2 'Nifty BeES AUM ₹66,777 Cr' vs data_market.md T7 '~53,989 Cr - partially_verified'
findings.summary: Nifty BeES AUM is cited as ₹66,777 Cr in two domains but ~₹53,989 Cr in the project's own market data pack — a ~24% gap for the instrument sizing the whole ETF execution plan.
findings.short_summary: NIFTYBEES AUM disagrees ~24% between two designs and data pack
findings.failure_scenario: Two of three sources agree with each other but disagree with the (also imperfectly verified) data pack; the ADV/impact-cost sizing logic built on this number should not be run on two different AUM bases.
findings.suggested_fix: Pull the live NIFTYBEES AUM figure at go-live and use one number across all documents; prefer the verified data pack absent a fresher primary source.

findings.target: design_allocation.md §3.3 composite-benchmark rationale ('long-short → arbitrage + 50% Nifty')
findings.summary: Folding REITs/InvITs (vol ~14%) and half the Alternatives sleeve into a low-risk arbitrage proxy (vol ~1.4%) will structurally understate the composite benchmark's true risk/return, making reported alpha easier to earn than it should be.
findings.short_summary: REITs proxied by arbitrage understates benchmark risk
findings.failure_scenario: This is a benchmark-construction choice, not a data error, but it means reported alpha (+55bps Moderate, +45bps Aggressive) is partly an artifact of comparing a real REIT/alternatives sleeve against an unrealistically low-risk proxy for those same assets.
findings.suggested_fix: Benchmark REITs against the Nifty REITs & InvITs Index (as design_performance.md's Table 3 already correctly does) and alternatives against a PME/absolute-return proxy plus a stated hurdle, not against arbitrage.

findings.target: design_regulatory.md §1.5 'Custodian for securities... mandatory for PMs (historic <₹500 Cr AUM exemption; at ₹500 Cr+ it binds anyway)'
findings.summary: A specific custodian AUM-exemption threshold is asserted without corroboration anywhere in the verified fact pack.
findings.short_summary: Custodian AUM-exemption claim is unverified
findings.failure_scenario: data_facts.md is silent on any AUM-linked custodian exemption; this reads as designer recall rather than a sourced fact and could be wrong, affecting a go/no-go compliance item.
findings.suggested_fix: Verify this specific carve-out against the primary PMS Regulations custodian clause before the operating model relies on it, or drop the parenthetical.

findings.target: design_rebalancing.md [11] and design_selection.md §1.1 on 'SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026' (exit-load cut, BER, brokerage caps)
findings.summary: Both domains cite a 2026 MF regulatory overhaul not present in the verified fact pack, and the two domains state the brokerage-cap change inconsistently with each other.
findings.short_summary: 2026 MF Regs cited inconsistently, unverified in fact pack
findings.failure_scenario: data_facts.md explicitly says TER slabs were 'not found/verified this session'; rebalancing cites brokerage cuts 'to 6bps(cash)/2bps(derivatives)' while selection cites 'from 12bps to 6bps (derivatives 5→2bps)' — different starting points for the same claimed reform.
findings.suggested_fix: Verify this 2026 MF reform against a primary SEBI source (it feeds cost assumptions used throughout Allocation and Selection) and reconcile the conflicting 'before' figures.

findings.target: design_performance.md §3.5 Table 5 ('Total explicit + implicit ~97 + 45 tax') vs the R1→R2 worked bridge's exclusion of bid-ask/consent-latency
findings.summary: Table 5's cost/tax budget risks double-counting against the document's own R0-R4 waterfall, which already embeds bid-ask/impact and consent-latency cost inside R1.
findings.short_summary: Cost budget table risks double-counting costs already inside R1
findings.failure_scenario: Table 5 lists bid-ask (5bps) and consent-latency (15bps) inside the ~97bps headline, but the worked R1→R2 bridge explicitly excludes exactly those two items as already embedded in R1. A reader taking ~97bps as 'additional drag on top of R1' double-counts 20bps.
findings.suggested_fix: Relabel Table 5 as an informational TCO reference, or split explicitly into 'already inside R1' vs 'R1→R2 bridge' columns.

findings.target: design_regulatory.md §5.2 'expected cost of delay = |target-actual| weight × daily vol × sqrt(days)', repeated in design_rebalancing.md §1 and design_risk.md §2.7
findings.summary: The consent-latency 'cost' formula presents a symmetric 1-sigma dispersion measure as if it were a one-directional expected cost.
findings.short_summary: Consent-latency 'cost' conflates volatility with expected loss
findings.failure_scenario: In a genuinely symmetric random walk, the expected P&L cost of a pure timing delay is close to zero; what's real is tail/regret risk and the fact that IC calls are directional. The narrative language ('costs ₹79 lakh') reads as a certain cost rather than a dispersion estimate, which could mislead the IC or client.
findings.suggested_fix: Reframe as 'consent-latency risk (1-sigma dispersion)' throughout and separately quantify directional opportunity cost using the IC's own tracked TAA hit rate.

findings.target: design_regulatory.md §2 ('Decision: Must [onboard as LVAI]') vs data_facts.md's caution that accreditation 'is not permanent... requires periodic renewal'
findings.summary: The mandate's entire consent architecture is built on the client's LVAI/accredited-investor status, but no document addresses what happens if that status lapses mid-mandate.
findings.short_summary: No contingency for LVAI accreditation lapsing mid-mandate
findings.failure_scenario: design_operations.md tracks 'accreditation status... validity date' as a field but no domain specifies whether the bespoke agreement (Schedule IV exemption, negotiated exit load) automatically reverts to standard PMS terms if not renewed, or whether a grace period exists.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit accreditation-lapse contingency clause to the NDPMS agreement and a renewal-tracking trigger (e.g. 90 days before expiry) to the operations calendar.

findings.target: design_allocation.md §5.3 ('Minimum trade size ₹1 Cr (20bps)') vs design_rebalancing.md §2.2 ('₹75 lakh–₹1 Cr (≈15-20bps)')
findings.summary: Minimum trade-size threshold is stated inconsistently between two domains.
findings.short_summary: Minimum trade size differs slightly between two docs
findings.failure_scenario: Minor documentation-hygiene inconsistency; the two figures are close enough not to change any decision, but should be unified.
findings.suggested_fix: Pick one number across both documents.

findings.target: design_risk.md §6 '10Y G-sec yield (current ~6.95-7.0% [design_allocation.md])' vs data_market.md T6 '>7.00%... 10-month high, verified'
findings.summary: The early-warning board's 10Y G-sec yield anchor is stale relative to the project's own verified snapshot.
findings.short_summary: Risk dashboard's 10Y G-sec anchor is stale vs verified data
findings.failure_scenario: Same root cause as the USDINR finding — a live dashboard citing a sibling design document instead of the verified data pack; small in magnitude here but part of a pattern.
findings.suggested_fix: Source dashboard reference anchors from data_market.md/a live feed, not from sibling design documents.

findings.target: design_selection.md §5.1 SIF-vs-Cat-III comparison ('Cat III... blended ≈28%')
findings.summary: The Cat III blended tax-rate assumption (~28%) is presented as settled without stating the income-mix assumption driving it.
findings.short_summary: Cat III tax-rate blend (28%) assumption not justified
findings.failure_scenario: A Cat III fund running more F&O/business income would push the effective rate toward MMR (~42.7%), reversing much of the modelled SIF advantage; real-world Cat III strategies vary widely on this axis.
findings.suggested_fix: State the assumed LTCG/STCG/business-income mix explicitly and show the comparison at both a 'mostly capital gains' and a 'mostly business income' Cat III fund.

findings.target: design_risk.md §1 Limit #10 (derivative notional) juxtaposing today's binding ceiling with the 2026 consultation-paper proposal in the same table row
findings.summary: Pipeline (not-yet-law) derivative limits sit inside the same hard-limit table as today's binding legal ceiling, distinguished only by a bracket.
findings.short_summary: Draft 2026 derivative limits sit inside the current hard-limit table
findings.failure_scenario: A reader skimming the table could mistake the 2026 proposal (1.25x exposure, 50% unhedged shorts) for current law despite the '(not yet notified)' caveat.
findings.suggested_fix: Move all '2026 proposal' figures out of hard-limit tables into a separate 'watch list' so current-law and pipeline numbers cannot be visually conflated.

top_missing_items: Accreditation-lapse contingency for the LVAI status the entire consent architecture depends on
NRI/FEMA branch logic for 'family accounts' and the international sleeve — no document asks whether any family member is an NRI, which would trigger a completely different FEMA/PMS regime
In-specie transfer-in / legacy-holdings transition plan — every deployment schedule assumes ~100% fresh cash, with no plan for a family transferring in existing concentrated positions
A single, reconciled Policy Composite benchmark with one named owner and sign-off date, rather than two conflicting tables inferred from Allocation and Performance
Data-privacy/DPDP Act 2023 compliance for the extensive PII/KYC/accreditation-certificate data architecture — entirely unaddressed
An explicit client liquidity/redemption-notice commitment (e.g. T+X days for up to Y% of AUM) given 12-15% of the book sits in 3-7-year locked AIFs
Suitability linkage from client risk-profile/horizon/liquidity-need questionnaire to the choice of Moderate (vs Aggressive) model for this specific family
A canonical, dated market-data snapshot that every domain cites from, instead of each domain quoting its own search-result Nifty/USDINR/10Y level on slightly different dates

Legal-entity/no-pooling compliance mapping for 'several family accounts... one Investment Approach' — PMS Regulations bar pooling, and per-account custody vs IA-level TWRR aggregation needs an explicit compliance walkthrough

Client-side succession/incapacity planning for the consent workflow (who holds power of attorney to approve an RPP if the client's signatory is unavailable), distinct from the 'unreachable during a tail event' protocol
A documented resolution path and single owner for the Reg 22 vs Reg 31 citation conflict and the unverified custodian-exemption/2026-MF-reform claims before any reach a client document or SEBI filing
what_is_strong: design_performance.md's Brinson-Fachler/Carino attribution worked example (§3.1, Table 4) — independently re-derived and exact to three decimal places; the R0-R4 return-series hierarchy (paper → gross → net → post-tax → post-tax-with-DTL) is genuinely good design the other domains should adopt.

design_risk.md's tail-hedge payoff table (§5.2) — the put-premium and payoff arithmetic across all eight historical episodes checks out exactly, with an honest 'running cost with no payoff in most years' conclusion rather than a hedging sales pitch.

The consent-latency framing threaded consistently through Regulatory, Rebalancing, Risk and Operations — correctly identifies NDPMS's real operating constraint (setting aside the volatility/cost conflation noted above).

design_regulatory.md's fact-verification discipline — flagging every unverified regulation sub-clause as 'verify', clearly separating the not-yet-notified 2026 consultation paper from current law, and data_facts.md's 'Things commonly believed but wrong' section.
design_selection.md's fee-layering rules (§9.1) and the direct-plan/no-distribution-fee discipline threaded through every instrument type — clean and completely defensible.

design_operations.md's four-eyes control table (§1.6) and the RPP→OMS foreign-key linkage ('an order cannot be released without a valid, unexpired, matching consent record') — the right architectural spine for proving NDPMS compliance at inspection.
